review:
Toby Fox probably did not expect the amount of love and tears this game would bring to the players, since his own description to advertise the game is unserious; joking about dating skeletons and dogs appearances. Yet the simplicity of his production reached millions of hearts in a way few games ever do.

At first glance, Undertale seems like a quirky, retro-style puzzle game . But it quickly becomes something more; a story about kindness, choice, and the consequences of your actions. It doesn’t just let you spare your enemies; it makes you wonder why you would want to hurt them in the first place. And somehow, in its quietest moments, it reaches your heart in the gentlest way.

Soundtracks are fun, super fun, a little sad, heartwarming, nostalgic to many, and so much more. I have a hard time not getting mist-eyed over ost 071 of this game, simply titled “Undertale”. This simple melodious and heartfelt ost is how Undertale feels, and what Undertale is. I retreat my words from earlier, probably Toby DID know how moving this experience would be, it just seems right to assume so, why would the most soul-stirring ost that you cant just simply ignore the tears building up as you listen, share the name of the game? 

I can’t believe this game is turning 10 years old this year, it takes me back so long ago, the old memes, the gameplays of many youtubers, people getting mad that Sans was hard to beat, the Amv’s, the AU’s, the AU’s soundtracks, the cringe OC’s that we used to meme about; you couldn’t escape the fandoms best and worst moments, I wonder if we were too judgmental on this cringey phase some in the fandom shared, we were younger, and much were just kids being kids that shared the same passion as the others. 

Now we look back with a nostalgic feeling, and i intend to always remember this game for what it was, for what it meant to many and to me, for what it offered and delivered, a fun, heartwarming, inspiring, engaging and beautiful experience, that brought me laughter and tears equally, rage too for many hehe.

Ten years of history and an unforgettable game that will be in our hearts as long as time goes by. Thank you Toby Fox, forever.❤️

Ten dollars. Only a few hours of gameplay. 16-bit graphics compared to the flashy 1080p stuff in standard games.

But... wow. Undertale blew me away. It doesn't need flashy graphics or even fanservice to falsify its enjoyment. It just does things right, and boy that was one immensely enjoyable experience.

I think most of the magic of this game comes from knowing absolutely nothing about it. I got this game from a friend and just decided to play it since it looked very interesting and it was getting good responses. So I went in completely blind, knowing nothing but the game's name. And I'm glad I did, because everything the game presented to me was unexpected, notably dark in places, and very emotional, which would have been lost entirely if i watched someone else play it. So, if you happened to have been flooded by everything Undertale on tumblr [strike](god help us)[/strike] and the entire story's already laid out for you, the magic has been lost and the game won't be as incredible of an experience. I'm sorry.

Of course, I call Undertale an "experience", not a game, only because it does such a fantastic job at it. Following the motto on the store page, "the game where you don't have to destroy anyone", the game always tries to nudge you in that direction, taking a back seat in your mind and reminding you to "Spare them!". And of course, you answer with "Why? Why should I do that when it offers me the option to kill anyone I want right in front of me? What's in it for me?" And that's where the game literally turns into a personal experience, as everyone has a different response for the game's selling point. And boy, does it turn to black or white pretty fast from here.

Undertale's ability to completely turn the tables of its story depending on your actions is massive. Upon your game's startup, every little thing you do will be set in stone in the game's story pathing. If you're the type who immerses yourself into the game's charming music, laughs at the childish but hiliarious anctics, and is willing to hork down healing items just to prevent yourself from killing a monster just because a fight is difficult, the game rewards you. It opens up a very character-developing and world-unfolding story, along with some of the most emotionally invested boss battles I have ever experienced. You know a game is good when it breaks the fourth wall so well that you're shaking in your seat in true fear and can't stop the shivers, all while having to fight a hopelessly overpowered god of a boss. The amazing writing only starts once you beat the final few bosses, and the story doesn't stop being good from there onwards.

On the other hand, what makes this game different is that it keeps its dark side from you, and its entirely your choice to experience it. If you scoff at the game's sparing choice since you're [i]too cool[/i] or [i]grown up[/i] to possibly be nice to people, you can go around and intentionally sink your weapon into a monster who just wants to be a friend. And unlike many other games, this isn't just a simple moment of "Oops, I killed another unnamed enemy, let's reset the game and nothing changes"... the weight of a dark choice is huge. Nothing can be taken back, and it forever changes your playthrough. Reset the game, and the characters know. Events change. And with each curious kill, you, in turn, turn from the only human in a land of monsters into the biggest monster in a land of innocents. In the end, ignoring what Undertale sets out to do, which is to let you experience childlike innocence and fun, only makes it delibrately change the game into a quieter, more grim story. Very little character development, and the world isn't explained to you, nothing. There's very little reward for going through this route. Yet it is a choice you can do. Granted, you get two of the hardest boss battles by becoming the murderer and will be forced into Game Overs repeatedly from them, but even that is a message from the game... [u]It's trying to stop you from getting to the end of this route. Before its too late.[/u]

It's as if you're doing deeds in an actual living, breathing world. And that's what makes it even more terrifying when you decide to become a murderer instead of a savior, because only you know that you're willingly going forward to obliterate every weakling in front of you. It's a test of your willpower, and it's your choice. The worst thing? The damage cannot be repaired. Go clean, or go home tainted. The game even gives you the choice to completely delete everyone's happiness after the most satisfying happy ending. The happiness you worked so hard to earn. And you can even become the murderer after saving the world, which will only permanently taint your game and never let you have a satisfying ending again. That's absolutely brutal, and yet that's still a choice. Amazing.

Yes, this game might not be for everyone. The humour may become dry after a while for some people, and tons of gamers nowadays like to bash at popular games instead of trying it out, just because they feel accomplished by doing it. But, if like me, you are willing to experience why everyone's been talking about this game, give it a shot. Hell, even if you hate the game to bits and want to kill everyone, buy the game, do so, and at least have your own personal experience before refunding it. This game does the morality concept so well that other games can only dream of doing the same, and it is one not to be forgotten.

It is a sin to call Undertale a game. Doing that would categorize Undertale into the bland and consequence-free "kill-em-all" genres that a lot of games are falling into now.

Undertale is a story-driven, emotional [b]experience[/b].

I hated Undertale.

It was, pretty clearly, a game about sexy skeletons. I did not care about sexy skeletons. I refused to play a game about sexy skeletons.

Then my friend made me listen to the soundtrack, and I decided I could deal with a few hours of sexy skeletons if I got to listen to the best video game music I had ever heard while doing it. 

I played Undertale. It's not a game about sexy skeletons. It's a game about choices, maybe, or morality, or curiosity. It's a game about pushing the limits. It's a game about experiences, about "what would happen if I did this?", about storytelling so intricate and complex and raw that it shouldn't be able to fit into seven hours of bullet hell and pixel graphics. But, somehow, it does. Every choice you make has an impact. Every object you check has a story. The soundtrack, the witty yet profound writing, the simple pixel graphics, and even the menu screens and bullet patterns themselves all intertwine in order to tell a story that only you decide the ending of.

Also, the skeletons aren't even sexy.

My advice to you: Go in as blind as you can. Don't read walkthroughs. Don't watch playthroughs. Don't prepare yourself. Don't even look at overviews. Hell, don't even read the Steam page description. Just buy the game (and give some well-earned money to a little white dog), and, as it were, climb the mountain yourself. Don't let anyone backseat. Don't listen to people who tell you there's a right way to play.

And when you think you've reached the end, just think--what other choices could you have made?

So, yes. I hated Undertale.

And then I played it.

[h1][b]Undertale...[/b][/h1] 

[i]Where do I even start with this game?*[/i] I feel like this is the type of game that everyone who loves video games has heard about, but not everyone has truly played. Sure, you might’ve seen the memes, the fan art, the endless discussions about the “pacifist” route vs. the “genocide” route, but [b][i]it’s the experience of actually playing it that hits you in a way that no amount of spoilers or reviews ever could[/i][/b]. Like, yeah, it’s a game, but [b]it’s also way more than that[/b]. [b][i][u]Undertale is a journey[/u][/i][/b]. [i]And a damn good one at that[/i].
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3461738426
Look, I’ve played my fair share of games. I’ve had my emotional moments. The highs, the lows, the victory, the defeat. But [i]Undertale did something[/i] that no other game has ever done for me: [b][i]it made me feel like my actions actually mattered[/i][/b]. I’ve never been forced to think so much about my choices in a game. Do I spare this monster? Do I show them kindness, even if it’s just a few words? Or do I give in to my darker impulses and kill them? The fact that [b]the game forces you to live with those choices[/b], that no matter what path you take, [b]the consequences hit home[/b]… it’s just something that so many other games miss. [i]Most games don’t ask you to actually feel the impact of your actions. [u]Undertale does[/u]. And that’s what makes it stand out.[/i]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3517859518
[b]It’s not trying to WOOOW you with high-end graphics or flashy cutscenes[/b]. Hell, the visuals are super basic, the characters are pixelated, but it doesn’t need all that. [b][i]The real strength of this game lies in how it uses the medium of video games to tell its story[/i][/b]. You’re not just a passive observer. You’re the one pulling the strings. The characters aren’t just there to look pretty or be generic NPCs – they have personalities, desires, fears, and they react to you. [i]The whole game feels like it’s speaking directly to you[/i], and that’s a rare thing to find in modern gaming.

[i]The humor, the heartache, the twists[/i] – [b]it’s all woven together so perfectly[/b] that I was laughing one moment and then tearing up the next. [i][u]Undertale knows how to balance its tones[/u][/i], something a lot of games can’t pull off. [i]It’s not just about having a good story [/i]– [b]it’s about how the story makes you feel[/b], and Undertale nails that in a way that very few games do.

[i]And the best part?*[/i] [b]You don’t need to play this game with any kind of guide or prior knowledge[/b]. Just dive in and let it take you wherever it wants to go. Every playthrough is different, and no matter how you approach it – pacifist, neutral, genocide – there’s something valuable to learn, something profound to experience. It’s not just a game. [i][b][u]It’s an experience that stays with you long after you’ve turned off the console[/u][/b][/i].
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3450456815
If you’ve somehow never played this game, do yourself a favor. Play it. Go in blind, with no expectations other than to see what unfolds. I promise you, this is a game that’s going to leave a mark on you. It’s the kind of game that makes you think about what it means to be human, to have choices, to live with the consequences. [b][i]A true masterpiece in every sense. 10/10[/i][/b], and I wouldn’t change a thing.

This is one of those few games that come along when times are bleak, and games have become regularly bland and heartless. Where you feel disenfranchised with the whole idea of video games. And you begin to start ask "Why?"... Like "Why should we play games?", "Why are games different from other media?", "Why should you use games as a form of expression?" and even "Why even play games at all?!" 

Undertale come along and says, "This is why."

When I first heard of Undertale, I had no interest in playing it. I thought the fanbase was massively cringeworthy and the game was probably uninteresting. 
I was correct about the fanbase, but boy was I wrong about the game. 

I normally play action/adventure RPG games with the occasional sprinkling of singleplayer FPS. I am not the kind of person to normally go in for conceptual hipster nonsense, and I say that because that's what I thought this game was. 

In reality, it has some of the best atmosphere and writing I've seen in a game in a very long time. And above all else, it manages to be heart-rendingly (no pun indended) sad at times and actually funny at other times. Plus, the music is fantastic and the whole package has a level of care I don't often see anymore. 

You are doing yourself a disservice if you don't try this game out. And I don't say that lightly.

Undertale is a game that has gained a considerable reputation, and even if you haven't played it, you've likely heard of it to some extent. While graphics and size are not the sole determinants of a game's quality, at first glance, it's hard to imagine how Undertale garnered so much praise with its seemingly simplistic graphics and "simple" gameplay. In reality, Undertale absolutely deserves all the praise it has received, and even now, many elements and its music continue to exude vitality in various other domains.

The game incorporates elements from traditional RPGs and Manic shooters in its gameplay, but what makes Undertale truly outstanding is not its gameplay but rather its storytelling and music. In terms of the story, Undertale presents players with a genuinely moving yet unconventional narrative about family, friendship, trust, and betrayal, employing a natural and unpretentious narrative approach. The game's interactivity is also remarkably high, allowing players to deeply experience the impact of their actions within the game and explore countless details to fully appreciate the game's charm. The characterization of the main characters in the game is vivid and lively, effectively showcasing their glamour. As for the music, Undertale's original and captivating soundtrack, combined with the game's storyline, provides players with a profound dual impact on their emotions and auditory senses.

No matter how exceptional a masterpiece may be, it is not exempt from criticism. However, in my view, this is not a game's flaw. Since the game's primary focus is almost entirely on crafting its narrative content, if you're not interested in most games' stories or cannot derive any emotional resonance from them, Undertale may not be suitable for you. Similarly, the game's systems are relatively intricate and complex, encompassing numerous puzzle-solving elements. Additionally, it deviates significantly from most typical RPG games, making the game much more challenging without guidance, and experiencing all the game's content in its entirety may require many meticulous operations. Furthermore, any spoilers regarding the game's plot can significantly undermine the gaming experience, putting players in a dilemma between relaxing walkthroughs and preserving the integrity of the experience. Certain routes in the game also pose considerable difficulty, rivaling that of hardcore Manic shooters, which may hinder all kinds of players from smoothly experiencing all of the game's content.

Undertale is an absolute must-play, worth experiencing for the majority of players. Please be careful not to get in touch with any game spoiler content, as it will greatly diminish the impact of the gaming experience. While it may require more time, it is undoubtedly worth it. If you don't enjoy narrative-driven games, dislike spending time exploring the game's content on your own, and don't enjoy empathizing with the game's characters, then Undertale may not be suitable for you.

Time is fake. Morality is optional. Started as a kind soul. Ended as a timeline-hopping war criminal (in game).

[hr][/hr] 
Started off thinking it was a cute little indie game. Ten minutes in, a goat mom offered me pie and unconditional love. Adorable. Accidentally killed someone? Congrats, now you’re on the Neutral route™. Got the "I'm not mad, just disappointed" speech by a skeleton and emotionally manipulated by a flower. Great.

Cue a reset and with that, True Pacifist. Spared everyone, became besties with a tall skeleton, a tuna with anger issues, a reptilian monster, etc. Got adopted by a goat mom and emotionally destroyed by backstory and friendship speeches. 10/10 therapy session.

Naturally, knowing that every choice I did altered the game, I followed up by murdering everything and everyone. Welcome to the Genocide Route, where you commit atrocities against monsterkind and the music slaps way too hard for how morally bankrupt you are. I defeated a skeleton, so he naturally decided to take my sanity. The game judged me. It remembers - forever.

Tried to be nice again. A red-eyed child decided we’re sharing a save file now - they remember. Cue the Soulless Pacifist run, where although you do everything right, the game remembers. Dust is stuck onto my hands. It'll never leave them.

[i] The flower still laughs. [/i]
[i] The save file still breathes. [/i]
[i] The pie’s still warm. [/i]

[hr][/hr] 
Play Undertale, they said. It’ll be fun, they said.
Now I sleep with one eye open and hear “MEGALOVANIA” in the walls.

I played Undertale years ago, back when I didn’t really know much about it. No spoilers, no deep dives into the fandom, not even a full grasp of the story. I just jumped in because I’d heard it was “different.” And it was. But now that I’ve grown and revisited it with fresh eyes and a better understanding of storytelling, game design, and emotional nuance… I get it. I finally get why this game is so widely loved. And honestly? It deserves every bit of that praise.

Looking back, I realize Undertale isn’t just a game you play. It’s a game that plays you. It watches, remembers, reacts. Your choices matter, and not in some artificial "good ending/bad ending" way—your choices feel personal. It makes you question who you are in a way few games even attempt.

I didn’t understand all that the first time. But now I do. And that’s why Undertale is a masterpiece. It’s not just a game. 

it’s an experience that grows with you. One that stays in your heart long after the final credits roll.

Some games are okay.

Some games make you stop and reevaluate who you are at the very core of your person, make you feel a depth of emotion that no work of art ever has before, and then leaves you with a genuine sense of loss when its all finally over and gone, because you know you won't ever be able to experience anything that beautiful for the first time ever again.

You should probably play Undertale and find out which one it is.

I first played Undertale eight years ago, and somehow it has never left me.

Beneath the humor, the weirdness, and the simple retro visuals is something deeply human. It is a story about empathy, seeing the humanity in evreyone, and realizing that every person you meet carries something worth understanding. It made me laugh in ways I did not expect, it made me think long after I stopped playing, and at times it genuinely caught me off guard emotionally.

Even now, all these years later, I still find myself going back to the soundtrack and remembering moments that somehow never lost their weight. Very few pieces of media have ever stayed with me like this.

It is fairly impossible to discuss Undertale and what it is, without discussing what it isn't. It truly isn't the most revolutionary game on its engine, but it did prove to be innovative. Toby Fox, a veteraned modder of Earthbound/Mother 3, who had cut his teeth with making ROM hacks, went on to make something truly interesting with Undertale.

Undertale is not so much a game, it is more a vehicle for a much larger fandom. And a fandom that has proven to be so significantly diverse, talented and at times, outright insane and intolerable, that it ironically had become the anti-thesis to the thesis of the game. But Undertale, itself, a game the embraces minimalism and yet, has ambitious, big ideas and remarkable presentation at the cost of anything being fairly high-brow, truly does something that few media forms can do. 

And that is give an entire generation of internet denizens schizophrenia. There was a time where you could not escape the Undertale memes. Even if you have never played Undertale, you sort of 'have' through symbiosis. Like background radiation, you have absorbed so much of this game without realizing it by simply being on the internet during a certain time. But to actually play and experience it for yourself is oddly intimate, despite it arguably being more enjoyable via vicariousness. 

When I lived in Denmark, ever briefly for three years, I more or less was attending the Viborg Animation Workshop, Graphic Storytelling course for free. I simply would just show up to classes, simply because I knew people there, as a perpetual 'guest' and while I would gain no credential, I would be surrounded by peers of the creative pursuits and arts. Not only that, but I got to meet many guest teachers from around the world, who made some significant IPs. Be they cartoons, be they comics... I also knew people who were studying 3D animation and modeling for video games and CGI special effects. 

But one person, I remembered very significantly was an Israeli man, who had boldly given up his Israeli citizenship for a Romanian one, just to get away from his country. His name was Tomer and he was gay. And he had a wicked sense of humour and some strong artistic direction with his own works. The man had also formerly been an Israeli commando and had grown to greatly resent this time in his life. Regardless of the details, he was an individual who was the embodiment of an art student. An open Marxist-Leninist. A conscious objector to the nation he was once born in and once served. And above all, a fan of Undertale.

A game he only played once.

I had played Undertale years prior around its release, inspired by videogamedunkey's video, which admittingly, spoiled a lot of the game. But I still enjoyed the humour and while it is far from my favourite game of this sort (Note, I am a huge fan of Fear and Hunger 1 and 2, which I've jokingly called "Undertale but good and edgy"), but what got me to REALLY play it again on this very steam account, having had to make a new one upon migrating to Denmark, was Tomer's unquestionable appreciation for his first playthrough.

A playthrough so absolute and impactful, blind and entirely driven by his own motivations to see it through for himself, that he wished to never play it again to preserve it a perfect memory. 

I had already forgotten some of the finer details in Undertale at this time and when I did go through it again, it clicked. And I 'got it'. My second playthrough of Undertale was 'that' play through, an experience of my own and one... I don't want to sully by playing again anytime soon.

Undertale is a psy op, a cult. A fandom that was vile, but also immensely impressive. Undertale has some immense flaws and some drawbacks, but it was made with passion. And frankly, love it, hate it. I recommend letting go of your vicarious enjoyment from memes and other people's opinions, do your best to just erase any memory of it and then play it blind without any worry of getting the best or worst ending. 

It is definitely one of the most games of all time. Toby Fox has dedicated himself to become a Yoko Taro-esque figure in recent years as he developed Deltarune, but it is cannot be understated how much he earned himself a spot in the unique zeitgeist of this era of the internet. 

Decades from now, this game will be remembered. And you will remember the people who remembered it before you played it even. A friend, now long gone and lost from this physical existence on Earth, once had her icon as Napstablook on skype. And I remember, with one of her quotes in her status, everyone was suddenly concerned for this person's mental health. Years later, we were certainly reminded that this was a healthy concern we should have kept up. 

Still, I will remember Undertale as a very strange experience that prominently will be bathed in nostalgia for a world that does not exist anymore. And memes left still quoted, but otherwise unspoken.

It was bigger than it deserved, but as satisfying than it needed to be. Just like your mum. Am I right lad, or am I right lads? (You are right lad)

When this little game rolled onto the Steam storefront on September 15th of 2015, I think it’s pretty safe to say hardly anyone probably could’ve imagined the impact it would have. I know I certainly didn’t; after all, my first exposure to Undertale came in the form of seeing the backlash its own fanbase brought upon it, alongside the vocal cynics and critics who panned it as “overrated garbage”. With claims flying left and right that it was the next Five Nights At Freddy’s and constant jokes about how it was “Tumblr’s favorite game”, I had plenty of reason to be skeptical.

When I looked into things myself, though, I found something far different than what I had been anticipating. Even from the very first moments I saw it in action, Undertale…connected with me, in a way few games have ever managed to, first impression or otherwise. As time continued on, I was shocked to see just how much love the game was receiving, including praise from such people as Totalbiscuit and Yahtzee (people known to have trouble enjoying most JRPGs), and so it rapidly became clear that there had to be something to this game; something big. If it could so thoroughly draw in even those who typically can’t enjoy the genre, then if nothing else, it had to be worth checking out.

I went in with some damn high expectations.
What I got was one of the best games I’ve ever played.

I truly wish I had the words to properly explain what Undertale is to me. I could go on for hours about the near-perfection of the soundtrack. I could rave about the writing and how rewardingly rich in detail and nuance it is. I could praise it for its characters and the level of care put into making even the most minor NPCs come to life with personality. I could write a freakin dissertation on the sheer brilliance of how it uses meta not only to comment on the tropes and conventions of its genre, but also as a powerful gameplay and storytelling tool that rewards replay value. I could gush until the end of time about the powerful messages Undertale presents and the skill with which it presents them, even addressing real world issues with an inspiring amount of dignity. 

However, what I truly adore the most about this game is how unapologetic it is. It’s never afraid to be what it is, and that confidence takes its strengths and makes them into something far greater than the sum of those parts. From start to finish, Undertale is one of the most utterly brilliant games I’ve ever seen, executed with a pitch-perfect prowess that creates an experience the likes of which few other games can match. 

There is always something new; another layer to be peeled back; another beautiful detail to be discovered. And the deeper one digs, the more brilliantly this absolute diamond of a gem sparkles. No part of Undertale is manufactured: not a single pixel has escaped the loving caress of a gentle crafting hand, and as the offspring of a mere $51,000 Kickstart (over 10x the amount Toby asked for), it’s easily one of the most refreshing games of the last few years. Undertale made me laugh. Undertale made me cry. Undertale made me think deeply about the world around me.

But most powerfully of all, Undertale touched me unlike any game before it. It's no small wonder, then, that upon completion it became my favorite game that I've ever played.

Yes indeed, this wonderfully unforgettable experience.

It fills me.
With determination.

I adore this game.

As a kid born with Devil May Cry, GTA, Resident Evil, and God of War, I never thought that text-based games like Undertale would be my kind of game. The simple graphics and heavy focus on story didn’t appeal to me at all. Plus, my English wasn’t great at the time, so I had no interest in trying it.

But eventually, many years later, I gave it a shot. And at first, I hated it; sorry about that, but for me, there was too much dialogue, which is technically still acceptable if most of the dialogue did not feel unnecessary and didn’t seem to affect the story. 

To clarify, if you're the type of person who loves diving deep into character backstories (such as learning about their favorite foods), you'll probably enjoy this aspect. But if you are that type of people who don't give a damn about other people's business (like me), sitting through their stories feels like pure torture as every time they open up, I will be like, “I don’t freakin care about what food you like to eat or what sport you prefer to watch, just tell me how to get the hell out of this damn place!”

However, as I played more, I realized that these little conversations gave the characters real personality, making the world feel alive rather than dull. This is when the magic begins; the more you play, the closer you get to each character. But still, if you really don't care about them, it's just putting useless information into your brain.

The combat was another surprise. It looked like a bunch of mini-games, but it actually required skill and attention. The game balanced story, dialogue, and gameplay better than I expected.

Still, I found it a bit too simplistic for my taste. The game relies heavily on reading, so this might not be for you if you’re not a fan of lengthy dialogues. 

Relying on reading is one thing, but the worst part is that stories lacked major twists or surprises, making the overall experience feel predictable, resulting in whatever you read becoming unnecessary information. I know this game has multiple endings, but that's not the point. The real issue is how predictable it is—"kill = bad" is way too simple. Games like Fallout or Elder Scrolls do it better, where choices aren’t clearly right or wrong, just shades of gray. Your actions don’t always lead to expected outcomes, and there’s no moral scoreboard judging you.

While it wasn’t my favorite, I can see why people love it—it’s unique, charming, and different from most games I’ve played.

So as you would expect I got the Leaderless ending and when I saw Sans tell me everything sucked and everyone wanted to die (I doubt thats correct but i could be wrong) I thought he would fight me. I got a little upset that I didn't get to fight sans and I hated the ending I got, I knew there was better endings I just didn't know how to get them. I spent a whole day playing my first run though which took around 6 hours, it was really long mainly because I looked at EVERYTHING. I like lore in games and when you can spend time talking and looking at everyone and everything it becomes fun and you get to know more of the story. The next day I went to go play Deltarune which was pretty good, I loved the jokes and I built an epic duck that exploded! I missed alot of things in the game too, but I just never felt like playing it again. As I finished Deltarune I knew what I wanted to do after, I came back to Undertale and started another playthrough. This time it was True Pacifist!

True Pacifist All The WAY!!!:

This playthrough added a new element to the game that made the fun factor go through the roof. Instead of killing everything I found new ways to befriend them and it made the story way more engaging. The game had touched me with its excellent writing of this unique cast of characters it has and the alternate ending of TP gave me the sniffles (it was prob my body telling me to "go to bed already"). The way the fight is presented and how you have to save your friends through this fight makes it super great and the music I swear Hopes and Dreams is the best song on the whole sound track hands down! There was only one more thing to do, it hurt pressing the true reset button but I knew what fate I had, I wasn't quitting intill I saw sans die.

I love the slowed down music and how dramatic the game acted when you killed all the monsters in an area. And my favorite thing of all, you instakill almost everything! Undyne the Undying was a really hard fight that forced me to focus super hard. Her different moves made it very difficult to kill her a second time. I eventually beat her but it forshadowed what Sans could be which made me want to fight him even more! I get to Sans after insta killing everything in Hotland and I swear he killed me 10+ times with his first move. He was tough as NAILS! I spent two hours trying to beat him and I eventually quit. The next day all i could think about was fighting Sans, as i get home from school its the first thing I do. I've ignored Undertale for longest time. Its fandom was already running rampart, and ignoring their overexaggeration, I thought Undertale was some underwhelming and generic RPG with dull graphics. But... Not until I tried it myself. I thought I would not struggle. I thought I would not shed a single tear to a game. I thought I won't be impressed. I was all wrong... So wrong... Undertale is truly a great indie title, like nothing seen before. There needs to be more games like it.
Now let's go to PROS and CONS, shall we?

PROS:
-Fighting is (mostly) optimal. There will be many parts where its focused on alternative ways of defeating your foe without killing it. It's what makes the game unique. It requires you to be creative and think freely in decision making.
-RPG - RNG = Undertale; Fighting and dodging mechanics are fair and fun.
-Although visuals look simplistic and pixelated, they are not as limited as seen. Prepare to see impressive stuff.
-Interesting puzzles to solve. Even in fights, you have to figure out what is required to spare characters.
-Quite entertaining humor. Sometimes well-thought out, sometimes just small comedy things that makes us smile.
-Loveable characters whose biographies and backstories are scattered around the world.
-Replayability and different endings.

(Small) CONS:
-Although the game bases on choices, some can feel really lack-luster. For example, killing some characters won't affect too much to the game. Killing or sparing everyone you encounter, however, makes big differences.
-Hard-to-come-by choices. Some choices can't be uncovered without trial-and-error. Completely new players won't be able to take every tinniest detail in consideration that it will affect the fate of characters, and it can lead to fatal mistakes and unwanted choices. On brighter side, it adds up as a bonus to replayability.
-Sparing random encounters are very unrewarding and difficult. It's much easier to slay them, as its only way to gain EXP and increase max HP, which will be extremely helpful when wanting to spare major characters by tanking their attacks.
-Healing items have no limitations. Stacking on healing items will make fights easy, even better, when you can dodge majority of attacks. Even if you run out of healing items, the fights will be almost at end anyway.
-Bad currency balance and shops. Most of objects in shops can be found for free by exploring, and the OP healing items are really cheap, while the amount of gold you earn is rather big. Then, there are places that ask for way too much gold. I get that it's supposed to be a joke, but its been done more than once, it's not necessary.
-Useless items. Not counting the jokey ones, many items are just waste of gold and you can complete the game just fine without them. Some do have interesting concept (e.g. similar to in-battle stat buff items and berries from Pokemon), but, I never really seen a reason to buy and use them. Their upsides and downsides are all unbalanced. It's best to just stick to healing items.

Although seem like CONS are much bigger than PROS, but that's because constructive PROS might spoil fun. I HIGHLY RECOMMEND you try this game if you got money to spare, it can last +10 hours depending on how much you explore and/or replay, and it will turn your night into an unforgeable adventure. One more last thing: Don't let the game frighten you with its 4th wall breaking. Stay determined.

To attempt to review Undertale in 8000 characters or less is to articulate the entirety of Crime and Punishment in a single sound. It’s a fruitless exercise in which I only take part to stroke my own belief that I, like Raskolnikov himself, have some “new word” to say. As I write this I would like nothing more than to shatter my computer and pens and paper and never think about any of this ever again because I’ve been thinking about this game and about everything larger than it for several days now before I publish this review.

I’ll admit from the beginning; there is a part of my brain, perhaps even an entire half, that wants to give this game a negative review. I could say that the characters need more development and exposition, that the writing is simple for my liking, lacking the wordiness and depth of respected tomes of the past, with words finespun, laser-targeted to hit the desired meaning. The humor is occasionally a miss. Some jokes go on for too long, some seem too lodged in Internet culture. I could say that a few plot elements seemed incomplete, a couple valid questions or alternatives going unstated, unanswered. The gameplay is almost childishly simple. Not necessarily easy, of course.

I could analyze this game as a piece of art, whose meaning and form are under scrutiny, or as a product, an option to be chosen off the infinitely spanning shelf of “content” to be consumed. I could treat it specially because of its age, or because of its youth. An interesting graph to look at on Wikipedia is the number of games published on Steam every year: 2015, the year of Undertale’s creation, represents the second major yearly step of growth on this graph, leading into a subsequent explosion of games that continues to this day: the so-called indiepocalypse. Perhaps the reason this game received such love at the time was because there were simply less games to go around. Perhaps not as many indie developers at the time tried as hard as Mr. Fox to produce their games. I don’t know. I don’t play a tremendous number of especially modern games. The prevailing winds of the indie game industry as I write this review are a number of low effort gambling related games and the genre affectionately referred to as “friendslop”. I’ve always preferred singleplayer games, and solitude, and reading classic books performatively (so I can make subpar literary allusions in my Steam reviews). So it goes.

And yet when I look inward, I see two halves revealed. There is the aforementioned half of my soul that declares that this game is almost childish, naive, under the false impression that even the worst among us have the ability to learn love and mercy and hope within their lives, chuckling at the mere belief that nobody in such an indifferent, absurdist world has to be deemed lost for even the most horrible actions. It is a soul of experience.

And yet, standing in the reflection of the mirror is a younger version of myself. One who hopes, and believes that all can be forgiven, that every other cheek can be turned, who is certain that a benevolent God is out there. I still carry a piece of that version of myself, like a fragment of a snowman, all throughout my life. A naivety, a desire to make sense of all the noise, to forgive and forgive.

In a world that can seem so bitter, so driven by spite and greed and lust for power and wealth, a world designed, seemingly openly and without any remorse, by computer algorithms tailored towards the principles of increasing user time on platform and ragebaiting to farm engagement, where compromise is viewed as impossible, where it feels that the world is steadily being sucked up by the digital era, by the internet and by laptops and phones and dual monitor setups that burn our eyes out and turn us against one another, in a world where so many people claim to lack a real voice, a game like Undertale is a piece of butterscotch-cinnamon pie.

Butterscotch is not my favorite flavor, I much prefer cinnamon on its own. I would love if Undertale was written with the magical realism of Márquez’s [i]Hundred Years of Solitude[/i], or the quiet solitude of Pamuk’s [i]Snow[/i], or the determination (!) of Camus’s [i]Stranger[/i], who persists like Sisyphus himself, who one of course must imagine happy. I wish that Undertale was written with the hope of Dostoevsky, whose novels, despite the often tear-jerking tragedies within them, often end with the ultimate sense that good shall prevail, even in a world so many consider to be so cruel. I wish that Undertale’s unsettling moments were written with the terror and uncomfortable structure of Krasznahorkai, or the same fear of the incomprehensible unknown as [i]Roadside Picnic[/i]. I wish its humor was more Three Stooge-ery, or more Seinfeld-y, or more akin to Gaidai’s comedy films of the 60s and their subtle political jabs and overt anti-alcoholism, because, while I hopefully have a lot more life to live, I do have a knowledge of what I’ve liked. From that knowledge, I must point out that Undertale's writing and story are not exactly Nobel Prize winning, no matter what anyone says. But it serves its purpose decently enough. And there is one thing, one particularly strong bit of cinnamon, in Undertale that I know without a shadow of doubt I liked...

Undertale has the best soundtrack of any game, no… likely any [i]piece of media[/i] I have ever consumed. Undertale is like a 5 or 6/10 if the music was even half as good as it is. If I listened to this game on mute, my jaded side might have won and given it a negative review, and called it overhyped: "Just buy the soundtrack on Bandcamp and ignore the game."

But you could pull shrapnel and broken glass out of my body and limbs without anesthesia in a dirty, fetid trench in Verdun during a World War I mustard gas attack and blast Sword of Justice, or Spider Dance, or Death by Glamour and I would still have a decent experience… how do you say that even an otherwise awful game (which Undertale is not) that one makes such a remark about is “not recommended?” In my opinion, there may never be another soundtrack like Undertale’s within my life. It’s frankly ASTONISHING how many pieces of music I heard before playing this game and recognized, even less memorable tunes that I thought were just free stock music that every YouTuber used because they were free or some other excuse… no, they come from here! Undertale may not be the best game I’ve ever played, but Toby Fox can take credit for seemingly creating half the soundtrack of the contemporary internet. And for that, I cannot express the level of credit that he ultimately must receive.

I recommend this game to just about anyone. Don’t read guides, or go looking for help in places where a spoiler might be revealed. Putting this game off and existing on the internet for 11 years, I must admit I already knew a great deal of the plot, of the things that made it powerful for those fortunate to be able to play it when it released. So much so that I honestly felt like I was replaying it in a way. And similarly, the more time you put off, the more things that made this game original become commonplace, mainstream. Jokes, mechanics, twists, all buried under a sea of titles that drew from its wake.

Perhaps you will scoff, say “this game just isn’t for me!” and decide you don’t like it. Perhaps you will become obsessed with it, ignore its flaws and consider it sacred, along with everything else Toby makes. I do not recommend either of these paths. Ultimately this game is a piece of art, not a multiplayer shooter or $80 sports game you buy every year so you don’t have to be alone with your thoughts when you get home from work every day, nor is it a MMORPG to sink thousands of hours into for similar purposes. It is to be enjoyed and critiqued for what it is, and what it is not. But the fact that I have this much to say about it should remove any doubt that it is worth your full consideration in the end.

It looks like just another strange indie game. And to be fair, it is a weird indie game. I mean, it is developed by a guy who made strange Earthbound Rom Hacks while being a Teenager and there is also a lot of Influence of the Mother (Earthbound) Saga in this game as well. It looks simple, almost deliberately underwhelming in its presentation, but t is a game that both understands traditional JRPG design and intentionally subverts it. And it trolls you. All the time.

In most RPGs, players are encouraged to defeat enemies, gather experience, level up, and grow stronger. It's a natural rhythm of gameplay we've grown used to. Undertale questions this pattern and forces players to stop and think about why they're doing what they're doing. Every encounter in the game gives you a choice: fight or spare. You can talk your way out of combat, calm enemies down, or find peaceful solutions in unexpected ways. The game not only allows this, it responds to it. Your decisions are remembered even across new playthroughs after the game has been finished. It doesn't just track your choices; it holds you accountable for them.

Combat itself is another area where Undertale strays from genre norms. Instead of passive turn based mechanics you need to dodge enemy attacks in real time, almost like a bullet hell game. This system brings variety to each battle, making every battle unique and it can make them genuinely challenging, often requiring several attempts to succeed.

Character and story writing is also a strong aspect of the game. It is narrative driven, and it becomes clear fairly quickly just how carefully it's all been constructed. It is consistent, the world feels cohesive, and the characters are not only memorable but often quite emotionally engaging. Despite the minimalistic graphics, there's a surprising amount of atmosphere here partly due to the writing, partly due to the music, and partly due to how the game uses its simplicity to its advantage.

Visually, Undertale is very basic. It uses a pixel art style that looks dated but has a distinct charm of its own. It's not visually impressive in any traditional sense bu the aesthetic serves the tone and themes well. The music, composed by Toby Fox, stands out more. It relies heavily on chiptune influences and catchy motifs, and many of the tracks are instantly recognizable and delivering much of the emotions you have in this game. The soundtrack plays a major role in setting the mood throughout the game. And Toby's Tracks can also be found in greater Nintendo Franchises like Pokémon Games or Super Smash Bros.

All in all, it's a great and fun game. You should get it, because it is definitly worth to check it out for yourself, when you are curious about it. Why are you still reading this, get it already!

Fuck. This is a tough one to write, not at all like my usual reviews. I'm just sort of rambling and gushing because there's so much to say about Undertale... and I can't SAY anything without spoiling the experience for you!

Yes, you!

Buy this game, don't watch anything on YouTube about it, don't read the Undertale subreddit or any wikis, don't even read this review (though I've avoided spoilers, of course) – just seal yourself into a room with a computer and some kind of makeshift toilet, play it to completion, clean yourself for the love of God, and come back.

...

Hero? Villain? Or something wholly other?

The year isn't out and there are some huge releases yet to come, but that being said...

Undertale is a GOTY contender, indie or otherwise. 

It's the best RPG in a year of amazing RPG releases. 

It's the funniest, most well-written game in, well, a very long time. 

It's the most genuinely heartwarming (and incredibly dark) game in, well, a very long time. 

It's challenging but surmountable, given a little skill and a whole lot of determination. 

And it's also the most mind-fucky game in, well, a very long time, in an entirely unique way! Sure, you can compare it to Metal Gear's Psycho Mantis or Eternal Darkness' sanity meter effects, though that won't do Undertale's special, thoughtful mechanics justice. 

But I digress.

You play as a tiny, gender-neutral child with bad fashion sense who falls down a mountain into a cavernous underworld filled with all sorts of fantastical monsters – all of whom have been banished there after losing a war with humankind. Now you have to get yourself back to the sunny, human-friendly overworld. 

Fairly standard so far, complete with the pretty concept art cutscenes and humdrum hero origin tale.

Then five minutes pass and all your expectations just sort of fly out the proverbial window screaming, never to return.

Like, ever.

Thus begins your six, seven, or eight hour (initial) journey into Undertale. You'll encounter all sorts of wacky, zany characters and monsters, puzzles, traditional RPG-type environments... loaded with obstacles standing between you and the finish line. And it's up to you decide how you're going to approach the aforementioned zany characters and monsters. Sure, you can do the traditional “kill indiscriminately” thing, but that's just one solution. See, Undertale is an RPG where you can beat the whole damn thing without killing anyone!

Like, you can hug your way through the entire affair!

Easy enough, right?

And you can always just reload a save if you screw up, right?

…

Anyhoo, combat mechanics are... it's hard to describe. It's like a traditional turn-based RPG combat system only, well, those expectations all went screaming out that window I mentioned earlier. Your heart appears in a window below the enemy you're currently dealing with and you have to dodge bullet-hell-style attacks... most of the time anyway. Even after your old expectations are but a distant memory, newly established expectations go flying out screaming too.

It's a little weird.

If fighting is your style you'll have that option, of course. Presented with a flashing bar, hit the sweet spot and you'll do the most possible damage; rinse and repeat. You can access items, check on the enemy's stats and what have you, pursue a peaceful resolution... lots of options, and every monster is a little different.

Well, not a little different – incredibly different, incredible variety! And figuring out their ticks, traits, fears, and dreams is all part of the fun puzzle that is Undertale. 

But there's more!

Undertale's music is fabulous – in that wonderfully synthetic, retro way. Every character has a “voice,” every monster, region, and special event has a theme, and when appropriate, the music is chillingly absent. It's the best part of this game - beside the top-notch writing.

I said every character has a “voice,” referring to the musical tones playing during dialogue. But they also each have their own VOICE, you understand? There's the overly protective mother, the bad jokester, the lacking-any-self-awareness fella... but even then it's just scratching the surface. These motherfuckers emote! These sprites have some Shakespearean depth that becomes more apparent with each hour, each playthrough. 

You'll care for them, whether you want to or not.

…


What else is there to say? I laughed out loud two dozen times or so, I lost count; I nearly cried at least five times, I was God damned jumpscared more than once, I had an existential crisis, and I'd do it all over again. 

And again.

And again. 

There's, like, nothing I can even complain about! Were some of the fights tedious, long-winded? Yeah, but I might be biased because I wanted to just enjoy more dialogue, more strange interactions, more environments. Were some of the references lost on me (particularly Anime stuff)? Sure, but that's what Google is for. 

Undertale just is... objectively good.

Objectively great.

It's an experience like Shadow of the Colossus, Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Half-Life, Red Dead Redemption, Dark Souls, EarthBound... a little, unassuming 2D RPG game released in 2015 stands shoulder to shoulder with some of the best games of all time – one I initially judged by its cover and ignored. 

I'm glad I deleted that particular corrupted save file and started fresh, because missing out on this game would have left a little heart-shaped void that I might have never filled.

Undertale. What to like about this game? Warning, Undertale is best played without ANY prior information. GO IN BLIND. Then you will understand what the game truly is.

-The Morality System: Your every action has consequenses. Unless you go into the game's files, the game could potentially remember you killing a single enemy and then reseting 100 times. The Game is not afraid to shatter the fourth wall, and when it does, it does so with glee.

-The Combat System: The game is a combination of traditional RPGs and Bullet-Hell shooters. You can dodge every attack if you are good enough. Also, with the ability to spare of kill any Monster you encounter, it challenges what we think of as good RPGs.

-The Story: While the story is basic at first, it is more about the characters you meet along the way. Flowey, the master of fourth wall breaking and a terrifying creature. Toriel, the motherly character who will do anything to protect you. Sans, a skeleton armed with bad puns and bad times. Papyrus, the brother of Sans who will do anything to join the Royal Guard and loves cooking spaghetti. Undyne, the leader of the Royal Guard with a hotheaded personality. Alphys, the Royal Scientist with a dark secret and a passion for Anime. Mettaton, the Killer Robot TV Host. Asgore, the king of all Monsters. Not to mention each Monster in a battle has a personality.

-The Endings: Neutral, Pacifist, and Genocide. The Three endings. I can't spoil to much, except that each ending accomplishes very different things. For Example, while Pacifist gives you a feeling of happiness, Genocide is physically and Mentally exhausting. In Genocide, you're gonna have a bad time.

-The Music: Oh My Days, the Music. Beautiful in every way.

Is this a good game? Yes. This surpassed all my expectations. 10/10.

How do I explain this game? Its like trying to describe a sunset to the blind. There's no *real* way reading any review or explanation could give you the exact feeling playing this game gives you. But I'll try to give you an idea.

When I first saw the trailer and heard of it I skipped past it a bunch. Sure I heard it was a good game, but it was some wierd 16bit thing. I'd rather play GTAV right?

Boy was I wrong.

So it comes on sale and I grab it out of sheer curiosity. Man was I in for a treat. The game itself is mechanically simple. You avoid enemy attacks with your red heart as enemies shoot varying behaving projectiles at you and then fire back by either using the "fight" option or the "act" option.

Its how the game handles the aftermath that makes it special. Kill a monster? It remembers that. Regret it and reload the game? The game remembers that too. You grow attached to these underground dwelling monsters, from the silly innocent Papyrus to the brave Undyne. I'm going to avoid spoilers as to how these characters develop but suffice it to say that they are all unique, likeable, and everyone is going to have their favorite. No monster down here in the underground is easily classified under evil or good. They all have stories. They all have reasons for the way they are. 

The graphics aren't anything special but they don't *need* to be. This is a game about a story. This is a game where you can write [b]your own[/b] story. Do you want to be the angel that saves the monsters, or the demon that destroys them? Do you want to crown someone king? Or do you wish to make no friends and simply leave this underground place.

All that can be done. By your choices. By your actions.

Don't take my word for it. I know you've been skipping past this game awhile. Maybe you keep seeing it in your front page and go "Ugh! I already know about this game!"

Do yourself a favor. Buy it. Its worth every dollar spent and you'll remember this game for the rest of your life.

A bit late to the party (half a decade or so to be exact). But what a journey.  Toby Fox thought of everything. I'm amazed at just how detailed the game is despite its seemingly simple premise and graphics on the surface. 

I went into this blind for my first playthrough, which is the best way to explore the game for the first time. So for any new players out there (if there are even any anymore), play the game the way you think it should be played. However, since this game really isn't meant to be played only once, it might get confusing once you've finished your first run, like it was for me. 

How many times you should play this game really depends on your intentions and how much time you're willing to spend. Sooner or later you'll want to go around looking for clues on how to beat the game after the first time if you're having a hard time figuring out what to do next. In my personal opinion, a bare minimum of two runs would be enough to get the best out of the game if you're only playing for the story. Three if you want the full Undertale experience.

Anyhow, Undertale is truly one of its kind, and is praiseworthy enough for its concept and storytelling alone. And with the range of emotions that the soundtracks on this game make you feel, it's just a truly wonderful experience. Sale or no sale, definitely worth your time and money.

I had to see what all the hype was about. How could this little indie game have better reviews than The Witcher 3? Honestly, I was very skeptical going in.

But I was *DETERMINED* to finish so that I could say I'd beat it when I wrote the negative review I was planning. So, I kept playing.

But then something happened... The game started breaking the 4th wall... The game began to blow my mind...  My knuckles were white from how intense the bullet-hell battles were becoming... The charm and quirkiness that had annoyed me in the beginning was now the cause of the permanent grin plastered on my face as I played... 

In the end, I must confess: The people are right. The hype is not empty. Undertale deserves all the love.

[h1]This game must be played from start to finish[/h1]

Undertale is an RPG game in which we control a hero who has found himself underground and is trying to return to the surface. In order to do this, he will have to traverse the levels of the underground world, where he will meet many different characters, friendly towards our character, but also those who will want to kill us at all costs. The problem is that our character is a human and only monsters live in the underworld, which does not put us in a very comfortable situation. It will put us in many uncomfortable situations from which we will have to find a convenient way out. Turning on the game for the first time may lead us to be perplexed as to why this game is so well regarded, what is so special about it, after all it is a fairly simply made game similar to those coming out before 2000. But Undertale does everything so well that today it's a cult game and shows that sometimes you don't need photorealistic graphics and beautiful animations, but it's enough to create a game with a great gameplay that we will remember for a long time and not forget about it right after finishing.

[h1]Fight or flight?[/h1]

Starting with the gameplay, as it is in an RPG we have a character level, equipment, and battles with enemies allow us to attack them, use found or bought items or escape from the battlefield. We can kill our opponents is logical, after all it is an RPG, but what if I told you that we can defeat any opponent without fighting? That's what Undertale enables us to do. However, if we choose to have a typical fight with our opponent then we have to be prepared for short, arcade games where we can lose some of our lives or even die. These are unique to all characters, so each, newly encountered opponent will be something new.

[h1]Simple but nice[/h1]

Moving on to the graphics we will see pixels, lots of pixels. But underneath those pixels are really a lot of interesting locations, characters that we will remember for a long time. Everything looks as if it fits together perfectly. At the beginning, the graphics can be disturbing, but after just a few minutes we forget about them, because the plot and the whole world take over here. Of course, we forget, but in the sense that instead of being a nuisance it becomes an element that we get used to and appreciate the longer we play. It becomes an important, integral part of our journey.

[h1]Music to my ears[/h1]

Just like the music. It's not as if the same soundtrack is playing all the time. Here, depending on the location or the enemy, you will hear something different. The music is catchy, even after finishing the game many of the tracks stayed in my memory. If the game has a gloomy atmosphere, the music also refers to this atmosphere. It is logically interconnected and makes sense (or sans hehe) Here it is worth mentioning that the soundtrack was created by one person, i.e. the game's creator.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

One can talk about Undertale for a long time, list its advantages, but it's better to just buy it and play it, and then give your own opinion. It's definitely one of the best games I've played, although it's quite short, but it allows you to complete the game in several different ways. There will probably be quite a few people who won't like the graphics or too simple gameplay, but I think the game is worth the price and worth giving it a chance.

After 10 years of this game being released, I finally played it on it's anniversary and not playing it sooner was the biggest regret of my life.

Undertale at first felt simple, and simple things aren't so bad. But it's entirely abstract as you put more time into the game and then it hits you so hard in the feels. What hit me the most was how much the game actually cares about your choices. Not in the usual "good vs evil" way, but in a way that makes you stop and think about why you're doing what you're doing. Every encounter felt meaningful. Every character felt like more than just an obstacle. They actually feel like real individuals, who you try to do right by. The music also deserves it's own mention, for it is just a soundtrack that will hit you by surprise as you move further into the story.

I experienced the true ending of this game, and it made me feel reflective. I wish I could experience it again, and I wish I had never "accidentally" killed the Royal Guards. ❤️ (also wowie my first steam review!!)
Gonna resist the temptation to write a whole essay here because nobody's actually gonna read that anyways. If you like story-driven games you should play this.

Listen. You and I both know that if you're browsing reviews and haven't played Undertale yet, you've probably seen or heard things that summon a bad taste in your mouth just from hearing the name. I was fortunate enough to play the game very shortly after it was released, and it was one of my favorite gaming experiences since I first picked up a GameBoy 20 years ago. It's no easy task to isolate the game from all the negative stigmas surrounding it that have arisen over the years, and I feel bad for all the people who have been turned away because of such things, but if you try your best to push all that aside you'll find fun characters, quirky gameplay, and spectacular music that come together to tell an amazing story that I don't think anyone should miss.

Undertale is an AMAZING game.
I had only seen its game reviews and gameplay on youtube previously and seeing it on summer sale, I decided to buy it. 

The story is insanely good. The choices you make in the game also affect the story which consists of 3 main routes which you can take. The death of any random character can make a difference in the dialogues in the game. Every major character has a background story to them which you can read through their dialogues. At times you feel bad for your enemies, feel empathy among other things. 

The gameplay is really really fun. I never felt a moment of boredom during my playthrough of the game. The battles are all different and you have to really try hard in some boss battles such as sans and undyne the undying. The game is full of mysteries and easter eggs which you can find and be amazed at. 

The game has amazing soundtracks which differ based on battles and area. The game is definitely worth the 10$ without sale and 3$ as of the summer sale 2021. I would be willing to pay even 20$ for this game.

The game is a MUST HAVE for anyone who likes ANY type of video games.

This game was a 10/10 for me.
